text_fidelity_a:
Merrithew at Home SPX Reformer Bundle There are several issues here to consider prior to purchasing.

1. Will the carriage roll smoothly? Even after cleaning the rails, my stott SPX failed to roll smoothly. This is a really important point.

2. Are the hand/foot loops large enough to accommodate normal sized, adult hands and feet? My stott SPX came with super tiny hand/feet loops that wouldn't work for a six year old, let alone an adult. And I have very small, adult hands.

3. Is the carriage padding sufficient? My stott SPX arrived with very thin padding and it hurt the back during movements.

4. Is this the best price on the market? Absolutely not. This package sells elsewhere on the internet for up to $500 less with additional dvd's included.

5. Will stott respond to inquiries? My phone calls and emails were ignored. It's as if this company only responds to large commercial accounts. You're completely on your own and out of luck if there is a problem or if you have a question.

6. Is the delivery box manageable? My stott SPX came in one box, approximately 14 feet long. Inside this massive box there were a couple smaller boxes. But you're talking something akin to tremendous problems getting it from curbside into the house, and if like me, you return it for being an incredible waste of money and a huge disappointment, it is painful to deal with a 14 foot box that won't fit into any normal car or suv. Hope you have a truck handy.

7. Check out other reformer brands. For a little more money the quality soars. You might think cheap is ok now, but you won't use a poor quality reformer in the long run.
text_fidelity_b: Merrithew at Home SPX Reformer Bundle

text_fidelity_a:
Princeton Tec AMP 1.0 Dive Light Accessory Cone - Replacement Parts I guess this would be useful for certain purposes. It turns the great AMP 1 LED flashlight into an "area" light. You get a uniform but relatively small area light and a small spot that shines through the tip of the cone.. The cone is thickly "frosted" and as an area light yeah maybe in a small two person tent. This diffuses the light and could be useful in a 3-5 foot range but of course more in total darkness, Outdoors at night with ambient light (starlight/moonlight-city lights) it does not do well at all. In total darkness it works fairly well, I got 7+ feet decent 360 degree area light though not too much more. Does not stay on very well. If you bump/drop it (even on carpet) or put it in a pocket, camping/gear bag etc. it will come off.

So the pros: Allows you the option of an small area light if you already have the AMP 1 LED flashlight. Small lightweight cone, easy to carry. Really a potentially good backpacking/light camping light, as you get 2 for one/flashlight(if you already have it ) and small area light "conversion". Feels pretty sturdy, not likely to get crushed in a gear bag. Diffused light not harsh on the eyes.

The cons: Not super bright, limited application. Does not attach/stay on very well. Easy to lose. 6-7 bucks for a buck worth of plastic.
text_fidelity_b: Princeton Tec AMP 1.0 Dive Light Accessory Cone - Replacement Parts

text_fidelity_a: Tents for Camping- 4/6 Person Anti-UV Sunscreen Instant Tent, Easy Quick Set Up Tent, Waterproof Camping Tent, Perfect Shelters for Adult Outdoor, Hunting, Fishing, Hiking, Backpacking I still have a "throw" one that's just like the window screen I use in my car - the kind that literally pops open and up.  It's small, but if I'm going to be out for just a night, like joining some friends at a nearby campground for someone's birthday or something, it is adequate, but if I'm going camping myself which is usually a 3-4 day thing, I want a tent that is more comfortable for me to spend time in/around.  That, is THIS ONE!  First, being able to more or less STAND UP inside a tent is a MUST for me.  I'm older and crawling around on the floor, trying to literally crab-walk out just to stand up - no...I want to be able to get up on two feet inside the tent and be able to walk out of it.  I may have to bend my head a little bit, but with this tent and my height, that's not much.  Okay, the other part about this tent is how FAST it goes up - like wicked-fast!  That sold me on this being THE tent for me - and then having the canopy for sitting in shade - this is perfect, just the one for me.  Okay, so this says 4/6 people and I am a person camping alone, but that's okay, I like having a roomy tent.  I'm not a hiker going off into the wild back-country having to tote everything on my back.  I drive into a campground of a national park and set up in a camping area.  So for me, taking this from the backseat or trunk of my car and setting it up on my campsite is easy-peasy.  Put my air mattress on the floor, sleeping bag on top of the air mattress, then set up my chair and I'm good to go!  Then it's time to go to the lake or take a walk on a nearby trail knowing my tent is up and everything is ready when I come back!

Men Waders Waterproof Chest Waders Bootfoot Chest Wader Light Hunting Fly Fishing Waders for Men with Boots Nylon/PVC Wader Camouflage/Brown 8-14 Seems like a few fake reviews on these... how 'bout a real one?

I bought these for a week-long trip to Alaska for salmon fishing on the lower Kenai River. My expectation was that I would throw them out at the end of the trip - instead I brought them home. They mostly met my expectations but are not a 5-star product.

Cons:
- The boots fit fine, sure, but the waders were otherwise too small. I'm 6'1, 270 lbs with a 55" beer gut, and have a 33-1/2 inseam. The bottoms went up to my crotch with a little slack, but the top and suspender straps are way too short. I had the buckles on the straps adjusted to the longest length without them constantly coming out (they did occasionally) and the straps really dug in to my shoulders. The straps should be at least six inches longer, but even better the upper part of the waders should be six inches taller. It was a bit of work to get them over my belly but I got to where I could do it over a hoodie and they were snug but not tight. If your inseam is longer than 34" and you're not going to get at least size 13, these won't fit.
- I could stand in them, but crouching or sitting without keeping my legs straight was impossible. There's no stretch in the fabric.
- The top of the pocket on mine is at my navel. Plus, no Velcro or snaps to keep it closed. I got river water inside, and constantly had things falling out. I lost a rented knife I had to replace and my $300 prescription sunglasses to the river.
- The boots don't have a comfortable insole and are really hard. I bought the $15 Dr. Scholls which worked fine.
- When standing in more than a foot of water the boot uppers would collapse and cause considerable pain to the tops of my feet, often to my toes.
- No breathability. My legs and lower trunk got nice and sweaty.

Pros:
+ All the joints are sealed and taped. I didn't have a drop of water on me from the outside.
+ Boots fit well.
+ Construction and materials are good for the price in my subjective opinion.

Neutral:
~ They are unlined. I knew this before buying them. Even wearing jeans my legs got really cold. Plan appropriately.

I wish someone had written a similar review before I bought these and had them arrive. I could have made the needed modifications before I left. With that said, I would not hesitate to buy these again or recommend them to a (very warm-blooded) friend.
text_fidelity_b: Men Waders Waterproof Chest Waders Bootfoot Chest Wader Light Hunting Fly Fishing Waders for Men with Boots Nylon/PVC Wader Camouflage/Brown 8-14

text_fidelity_a:
Case XX Sod Buster Jr. 00032 Knife This review is going to be biased. Can't be helped. My first three knives were a Barlow (a really cheap one) a Victorinox and a Case stockman (or was it a trapper) . Idk, my dad stole all of these from me when I got old enough to do any damage with them. The case is the only one I miss. I'm tempted, as a 40 year old grown man, to go rifling through his drawers to find it. And my pellet gun.
The Sodbuster is the biggest Case knife I've ever seen. My father-in-law carries a trapper and usually I got my Tx toothpick on me, but when I got this sucker, I was pretty impressed with its size. Let's get the obvious stuff out of the way, it's a slipjoint (a really easy one too), no pocket clip, no newfangled blade steel. It's a work knife for digging around in a garden. Some folks will be turned off by all of these things. I look at them as plusses. I'm not sure where the idea that a non-locking blade = dangerous came about. You really do have to handle slipjoints slightly differently than locking blades but they are just as safe if not safer in most contexts. It's a matter of exposure. I carved wood with my barlow for years, and occasionally the blade would stick or something but I always knew that could happen. I did have one close on my fingers once or twice but there wasn't any force behind it and not really anything happened as a result. I think most modern knife folks grew up with a slipjoint and maybe injured themselves with one as a kid, possibly while clowning around with it, to the point where as adults they think of them as an unnecessary hazard. The pocket clip... well I could take it or leave it. It's easier for a work knife not to have to fish around in my pocket for it repeatedly. That said, mostly I leave this one on my desk or table. Not sure I would carry it around in public. It's mighty big for a pocket. As for the blade steel, I generally prefer high carbon steel. I can sharpen such a knife really well with a stone. I'm not sure that I really like the edge retention of modern steels. I have an r2d2 - I have yet to sharpen it, but I'm guessing it will be a pain in the butt. I know exactly what to expect with softer steels.. In short, this is a fine knife appointed well for the last millenia. It's the folksier version of a RAT 1 and it will appeal to any who like the shape.
text_fidelity_b: Case XX Sod Buster Jr. 00032 Knife

text_fidelity_a:
Niceday Elliptical Machine, Elliptical Trainer for Home with Hyper-Quiet Magnetic Driving System, 16 Resistance Levels, 15.5IN Stride, 400LBS Weight Capacity Expect a BIG box to arrive! This sucker weighs about 100lbs. So you may need help to move it & get it unboxed.

The manufacturer states 90% assembled, but it's probably more like 50%. The flywheel & deck components will come pre-assembled. You are in charge of basically 5 main assembly groups: the feet/legs, the vertical tube screws, the handles, the console (computer) & finally the pedals. All tools are included to allow you to get right to work.

It's not a hard assembly, but the documentation isn't the easiest to follow. Luckily, the manufacturer has an assembly video on their Amazon listing. So if you need help, definitely check that out. In fact, you may want to watch it first.

The most cumbersome part of the assembly is the feet/legs. This is b/c you must hold up the entire unit (front or back) to get the respective leg on. If you have a helper, then this will be easy. If, however, you're a lone wolf, then use something to "jack" up the bike. It makes this part MUCH easier. I had a scrap piece of 2x4 that I used (see pic) & it was very helpful.

Once the feet are on, you will move on to the vertical tube screws, then handles, then console & lastly, the computer. Again, these are all very easy parts to put together. Just lay out all parts first, watch the video & review which bolt/screw goes where BEFORE you start the assembly. It will make a big difference towards minimizing your frustration.

Also, BE AWARE that some bolts ARE ALREADY PRE-SCREWED INTO THE BIKE. So they will not be in the bolt bag. For example, I found this was the case for the pulse handle.

Once assembled, the bike works exactly as advertised. It's near silent, very compact (for an elliptical), but still feels very roomy, has 16 levels of resistance (magnetic) controlled by an adjustment dial & has a number of functions & biometrics that can be tracked such as distance, calories burned, time, etc..

Please note - to track PULSE, you must hold the center handles (called the PULSE HANDLES) as there are sensors built in that your palms will contact. However, if you remove your grip, then the pulse biometric will disappear from the computer screen.

A more accurate method, would be to use a fitness tracker (like a FitBit, Apple Watch or dozens of other makes & models). This way you can track all of your stats in one place (steps, cals burned, distance, etc..) & have that data logged in your smartwatch app. Plus your stats will be far more accurate than the built-in computer on the bike.

However, for convenience & simplicity, the bike computer will do just fine. One option that I would have liked to have seen is a built in light in the LCD panel. If you're in a room with low light then the display can be hard to read.

It's worth mentioning that there's no external power required to run this bike. So you don't need to plug into an outlet. The computer will need 2x AA batteries. However, the manufacturer conveniently ships these with the bike.

So, to wrap things up, the build is going to take a little time, but nothing you can't handle! Once assembled, this bike is very comfortable to use & definitely feels well constructed for a consumer level elliptical. I think the price of $550 w/ free shipping (using Prime & a $50 coupon - at the time of this review) is very fair for this unit.

Overall, this is a great elliptical that will help you meet your daily step, cardio or high intensity workout goals. I definitely can recommend!
text_fidelity_b: Niceday Elliptical Machine, Elliptical Trainer for Home with Hyper-Quiet Magnetic Driving System, 16 Resistance Levels, 15.5IN Stride, 400LBS Weight Capacity

Gotrax scooter The first shipped scooter came with a snapped off rear fender in a nondescript cardboard box and looked used (sketchy). I contacted amazon and they provided a replacement scooter and a UPS pickup that I now had to worry about missing... Annoying, but whatever.

The second scooter came in COMPLETELY different packaging. Looked legit this time - graphics on the box, in plastic sheeting, etc. Just used the scooter to go about a mile each way (with hills) and it was fine for a 6ft 1in 190lb guy. Did use 1/4 of the battery doing so. The throttle and break levers both stick, so pay attention as it will continue to power even after letting go of the throttle and vise versa for the break. We shall see if it can stand the test of time. I did get the insurance as based off many reviews, this thing is not going to make it long, so I did want to be covered.

You are getting what you pay for here. DO NOT step on the rear fender and I would also not recommend folding, as it snaps onto and stresses the fragile rear (plastic) fender. They also structurally tied the rear foot breaking mechanism into the rear fender as well. Cannot stress enough how not strong and flimsy this rear fender situation is. However for whatever reason, it is an integral part of the functional design of the scooter in many ways. If it snapps off, you are done with the rear foot break.

However for the price, still throwing up 3 stars. Cant expect the world at this price point.
text_fidelity_b: Gotrax scooter

This cooler is incredibly well-made and I'm thrilled that I got it! (I ended up buying everyone their favorite team's cooler in this same brand, and they were a huge hit over the holidays!)

The first great surprise when it arrived was that it is made by Coleman, with tags on it to prove it. Coleman doesn't make bad stuff, in fact, they have a long history of well-made products, so that was a really nice bonus.

On top of that, there are all kinds of quality extras built into it. For example, when you lift the lid, there is a mesh ice-pack holder built right into the top of it. On the outside of it, there are mesh holders on each side (I use them for napkins, straws, or nutrition bars). I also got one of these coolers for a friend who is disabled and likes to keep a cooler next to her bed. Well, she'd gotten fed up with coolers that didn't keep things cold for very long and she had switched to using a spaghetti pot (for real!) with ice packs in it, to keep her ginger ale chilled, for constant nausea. She said that with a few frozen ice packs in it, she actually can go two whole days without having to replace the ice packs. She also said it fits great on her scooter when she's on the go.

Made by Coleman, like I said, and with lots of nice features, this high quality cooler is a must-have and a great gift. Check out the same cooler with other team logos. So basically it could go together a little quicker if you keep yourself organized. I recommend that you do the following . Remove all the pieces from packaging (assuring that you have all you are supposed to have). Match up all the screws and nuts to make sure you have good thread matching. This keeps you from dropping them and/or losing track in the midst of the assembly. The instructions are not the best I have seen but they do give you enough information to get the job done. The pieces seem to me to only have one way to put them together and if you have a remote idea (remember the instructions) it should go together rather quickly. Avoid tightening the nuts and screws completely until you have the all the screws and bolts for the pieces you are working on in place. When you do snug them up and move to the next piece. A couple of them will make you wish for a third arm but if you have someone there to lend a hand on the trickier ones, it should be a breeze. I was working on a carpeted area so I did some flipping around to help give me the angles I wanted. The carpet allowed me not to worry about scratching the floor or the metal. After putting this together, I think I could put one together in about twenty minutes without distraction.
I like the look of the organizer and it had plenty of room for my old Mizuno cart bag and my new Sun Mountain cart bag. It seems like it will be plenty durable although I guess that remains to be seen over time. It was light to move around (unloaded). I am most pleased with the end product.

text_fidelity_a:
ALEX Toys Little Jumpers Trampoline 786 I do not recommend the Alex Little Jumper Trampoline unless space is an issue. For $23 less you can purchase the significantly larger and more stable [[ASIN:B008BIV87M Bazoongi 48" Trampoline Bouncer with Easy Hold Handle Bar - Sunshine Yellow. Special Exclusive Limited Edition]].

The instructions are worthless. For example, one part states to "attach the bungee cord to the cord lock by pulling the knotted end of the cord tight". Can I just start by saying "What?" Well there is no knotted end, so you have to create it, though it doesn't really tell you how to do that. Then you have the issue of only three helpful images for the entire manual. And I probably need to start by saying I like to consider myself rather capable when it comes to assembling items and frames of structures having helped my father build our homes and additions. The instructions also do not elaborate where the knotted end should go in reference to the trampoline itself. You can figure out where it needs to go in the medal cord lock, but not on the trampoline itself. The only picture shows half of the trampoline having the cord wrapped around it so you are left wondering what the starting point looks like.

I hazarded a guess and just went with it at that point. Once I wrapped everything around and made sure that I pulled the cord tight several times I then tied it off. The instructions are then once again really vague; therefore I knotted the last end of the cord by itself and pulled it through the medal fastener. I then proceeded to knot the last end of the cord that I had just wrapped around with the beginning part of the cord to ensure an additional sense of security. The instructions mention nothing of this but after looking at the final results, with pieces of cord jutting out in random places, I knew that my three youngest would see that as an invitation to mess with it. So I knotted both ends together, and I did that twice. My kids can be rather problematic.

The directions then tell you to place the cover on the trampoline, making sure that it fits. Once again, the instructions lack on details. They do not specify that the cover should be placed in a specific direction. I used the writing on the cover as an indication for direction, placing the writing outwards where the handle will go. Otherwise, the cover does not fit. I found this out through trial and error, of course. There are also plastic clips that apparently must be clipped to the trampoline in some fashion, that you obviously have to figure out on your own. The most obvious thing was to clip them to the bungee cords that were wrapped around the trampoline.

The next step is to secure the handle. And yet again, those wonderful directions prove that they are pointless. I finally just put the small yellow bar into the curved handle portion (not attaching to the trampoline base yet) to get a sense of where it should go in the actual trampoline frame. I was then able to figure out which direction it faced, knowing that screws would be added at the end. REALLY not clear, but I was able to figure out having put together dozens of pieces before.

All in all, given that it was purchased at a discounted price, it will work out fine in addition to our other in home trampoline. This might be alright for one child, but it would definitely not work for my three kids (4 yr old twins and a 2 yr old) if I did not have the second larger trampoline. They are the ultimate test in terms of durability for any toy and this one is unfortunately not built for heavy duty usage. This might be fine on its own for occasional use from a calmer child, which none of mine are.
text_fidelity_b: ALEX Toys Little Jumpers Trampoline 786

text_fidelity_a:
Livestrong LS8.0E Elliptical Edited 2015

Since the first little hiccups, I haven't had a single problem. Tip - get a professional assemble - it will be worth it. I use it every day and love it - it is the best out there, especially in the price range !

The Pros: The design of the footbeds and stride is ergonomic and I have no joint pain when using it. The levels have sufficient range for absolute beginners to pretty fit people to get a good, safe workout. When working it was very quiet (must have a gym mat).'' Having an elliptical at home is the best.

The cons: There are constantly major things wrong with it (3 service calls in 5 months) and I had it professionally delivered and installed. I am 110 lbs and the only person who uses it. It has now been out of use 10% of the time I have had it. The bolts/bearings on the pivot arm were broken, the flywheel belt and now the flywheel itself. Customer service is disorganized and slow to respond. They have many subcontractors all over who do the fixing and the level of compentency is very variable (2 out of 3 very poor). I would never buy this again nor would I recommend it. Check out reviews from Dicks Sporting goods and other sites. The longevity of this machine is not good and the quality is variable - poor. 800$ is a lot of money to spend on 200lbs of something that I can't use.

Helpful Info about ellipticals in general: You should be aware that ellipticals weigh ~ 200 lbs. You should not only measure length and width at the base to see if it fits in your space, but the height (low ceiling basements will not work with a tall person). Also the area around the machine - how much room you want to the walls. I have a small space, but I wanted to be able to use weights to do upper body, so you need more arm spread .
text_fidelity_b: Livestrong LS8.0E Elliptical

text_fidelity_a:
HOMGIM Exercise Bike [[VIDEOID:bf4a381ea2346e023f15723581aa57ec]] This bike is easy to set up and adjust, and it has lots of features that make it a useful addition to my fitness program. I've uploaded a short video showing the adjustments and features, but I'll run thru them quickly here, too. Let me know if you find anything here useful.

You'll want to set the seat height so that your thigh) (hip to knee) is parallel to the ground at the top of the rotation. Then slide the seat back to where it's an easy reach forward to the handlebars without holding a lot of your weight there.

The tension on the pedals is adjusted by a big black knob just below the handlebars. There are also separate tensioned handles that you can pull to get an upper body (arms, shoulders, back, and abs) workout as you ride.

You can scroll through various screens on the electronic display. The best of these, in my opinion, is a heart rate monitor that reads your pulse while your hands are on the handlebar sensors. You can also get distance, time, and speed traveled. Its really a pretty capable machine, considering the low price.

This little bike folds up when not in use, so you can store it in a closet, lay it on the floor along a wall, or lean it in a corner. It isn't as beefy (or likely as durable) as one of the fancy spinning bikes at the gym, but this one is a lot more affordable, and meets my needs at home just fine. Check out the video, and let me know this was helpful.
text_fidelity_b: HOMGIM Exercise Bike

Solo Stove Campfire Camping Stove Portable Stove for Backpacking Outdoor Cooking Great Stainless Steel Camping Backpacking Stove Compact Wood Stove Design-No Batteries or Liquid Fuel Canisters Needed The third and largest in the all stainless Solo Stove line, the Campfire is perfect for replacing it's namesake traditional "campfire".
This past weekend I had a cookout with friends we had the Campfire and my friend had a propane grill.

While my friends grill was heating up, we quickly got a roaring file going in the Campfire. It was easy to set up and get going.
I keep a set of Fiskars pruning shears on hand to easily prep my stove fuel into about 4 inch length peices from downed tree limbs.

Start off with some small tinder in the bottom then a squirt of alcohol hand sanitizer as an accelerant, set it off with a lighter.

Begin adding on processed twigs from thinnest to thickest. I would say it was only about 5 minutes for the fire to get big enough
for the gassification effect to kick in and the blazing fire was eating the thicker branch peices with ease.

On this cold day we all enjyed standing around the Campfire to stay warm.

While my friend grilled burgers on his propane grill, we grilled onions and mushrooms in a veggie grilling basket on the Campfire.

We didn't want to fry the burgers in a pan and didnt want grill them over the Campfire because we didn't want to get grease all down in the Campfire.
When the fire burned out nothing was left but pure white as that was dumped out and mixed into the soil with a few good kicks.

The Campfire is too big as a backpacking stove, but is great for base camp stove or for backyard gathering.
When you want a campfire without a campfire ring and campfire mess, this is the ticket.

Highest quality product, highly recommended with no reservations!

text_fidelity_a: Garmin Varia RTL510, Bike/Cycling Radar Tail Light, Alerts for Rear-Approaching Vehicles This was made just for me.  My rides are on rural roads with narrow shoulders and little traffic. A rear view mirror is my primary defense and often I can hear the rare vehicles approaching. The Varia is a fantastic augmentation to keep me aware of vehicles coming up and works like a charm only because of the audio alert which the previous model did not have. I sewed the rear light (which is also great to keep me more visible) mount to the back of my under-the-seat bike bag.  I can't imagine an urban rider having as much success with this unit but I am thrilled to be using it.  Thanks Garmin.  The instructions on the Garmin website could have been clearer. Varia is a must have for riders with less frequent traffic and though pricey, it costs less than the deductible on my medical insurance if I were to have an accident.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Varia RTL510, Bike/Cycling Radar Tail Light, Alerts for Rear-Approaching Vehicles

We really only needed the low and medum settings. I'm very happy I opted for the insulated model. There was no condensation and no pesky dripping!! I'm also glad I got the drill bit to put in ice anchors. I suggest you get it too, putting in two anchors by hand will take you longer than setting the shack up. text_fidelity_a:
Stack-On PS-1520 Gun Safe I've had my safe for a couple weeks now and I am pretty happy with it. I was looking for an inexpensive safe to keep valuables away from the casual thief. This safe is not going to stop a professional thief. For that type of safe you need to pay upwards of $500. This safe is also not fire or waterproof so if you need those types of features look elsewhere.

The safe weighs about 40 pounds so it is critical to bolt it down, otherwise a thief can just walk off with it. There are 4 holes in the back of the safe and 4 holes in the bottom. There were 4 pretty hefty screws provided, I mounted my safe inside a large cabinet and it seems pretty secure. The safe and door are made of pretty heavy gauge steel so it is not going to be easy to just pry it open.

Inside the safe there are two metal shelves held in place by cheap plastic fasteners. But I will get into that later. Programming the security code was very easy and I had no problem opening and closing the safe. The safe also comes with two keys in case you forget your code or if the batteries die. There is a pretty loud beep when the buttons are pressed but that can be turned off.

I just have two minor issues with the safe. First, the cheap plastic fasteners used to hold the shelves in place are useless. When I opened the safe they were laying in the bottom of the safe with the shelves and half of them were broken. Easily resolved though, I just used metal bolts and screws I had to hold the shelves in place. I think manufacturer should provide these. The second issue I had was with the cheap shelf liners provided. They are very thin foam material and don't stay in place when sliding things in and out. Again though easily resolved by replacing with more substantial liner.

Overall I am pretty happy with this safe. I looked at others in the price range and many seemed to have significant quality issues. The issues I have with this safe are very minor and to be expected for a safe at this price point. This safe is a good value for your money as long as you are just looking to protect valuables from a casual thief
text_fidelity_b: Stack-On PS-1520 Gun Safe

text_fidelity_a:
Keystand Kids Snorkel Mask Full Face, Breathing Mechanism Snorkeling Masks, Flat Crystal Lens, 180° Panoramic Anti-Leak/Anti-Fog Mask and Snorkel with Detachable Camera Mount I've used a mask and snorkel for fun, for at least the last 50 years, and spent over 20 years as a professional scuba diver, as part of my job. I've always used a traditional mask for snorkeling and diving, and have had my share of leaky seals, fogged glass, broken hardware, and mouthfuls of salty water. This new generation of full-face masks with an integrated snorkel really does represent a breakthrough, in several respects.

I was intrigued when I first saw integrated full-face snorkel masks like this one a few years ago, and have finally decided to give one a try. I'm glad that I did.

There are many design features that really do make this snorkel mask a game changer for me. I particularly like the separate, sealed compartments that separate your eyes/cheeks/forehead from your nose and mouth. This minimizes fogging that can be caused by inadvertently breathing into a traditional mask through your nose, making it hard to see in the water. It also keeps any water that leaks in around your chin away from the glass that you see through. That's important to me, because I have a beard that does sometimes let water leak into my mask.

The seal on this mask is a soft, doubled-over flap that does an admirable job. I have a thin face and it is often difficult to find a mask that seals well. This one does. And it does a surprisingly good job sealing over my beard, which I try to keep short.

The air comes in through the top of the mask, and travels through one-way valves to the lower chamber where your mouth and nose are. Exhalations exit through purge valves near your jaw. This system works well, but I wish that the air opening at the top of the mask, where the snorkel enters, was larger. It sometimes feels like I have to work too hard to get a big breath of air, which can lead to a feeling of claustrophobia and, for some users, I expect, panic. A bigger airway would probably alleviate this.

There is a place to install a go-pro style action camera, which I will be using for sure. It's a thoughtful addition that will simplify saving and sharing my adventures.

The snorkel has a float valve that keeps water from flooding the mask when you dive. This sort of valve is great for playing near the surface, but probably not reliable for deep diving.

You can't use this mask for scuba diving, because there's no way to get your regulator into your mouth. For regular snorkeling though, I have a new favorite mask!
text_fidelity_b: Keystand Kids Snorkel Mask Full Face, Breathing Mechanism Snorkeling Masks, Flat Crystal Lens, 180° Panoramic Anti-Leak/Anti-Fog Mask and Snorkel with Detachable Camera Mount

text_fidelity_a:
GymPaws Real Leather Hand Pad Workout Glove Alternative | Hygienic n' Washable | Slightly Padded Palm w 4 Finger Loop SweatProof Back | Mens | Womens I gave up gloves about 10 years ago in favor of pads/grips. It felt odd at first, but after a few weeks, I realized that I could never go back to using gloves. Gloves were bulky, bunched in the wrong places, and made my hands too sweaty and hot. Pads/grips gave me protection without adding bulk, were easy to take on and off when necessary, and held up longer. The only thing I didn't like was that they had a single strap that went across the back of the hand. Even if I laced my fingers through the strap, I could never get a firm enough hold to keep them on for things like medicine ball work. Everything else -- dumbbells, barbells, rowing, push ups -- was fine. So when I lost those grips, I ordered GymPaws because I thought that the individual finger loops would make for a solid grip.

Unfortunately, the GymPaws weren't a good fit for me. On three of the four finger loops, I could see daylight between my fingers and the material -- not a lot but enough that I felt the pads sliding when trying to do some fast work with the medicine ball. So GymPaws were too big for my fingers, yet they were also too small for my palms. I'm a woman, about 5'2", and my hands are proportional to my size, though obviously smaller than many other people's hands. The brand I used before GymPaws provided more coverage on the palm, but the GymPaws left a bit too much skin exposed at the base of my thumb. It didn't prevent me from getting a solid grip on the dumbbells, barbell, or rower, but it was often irritating.

Making a product like this has got to be difficult because you can only make so many sizes and still keep the price affordable. Having one size only is the easiest way, but then it's, 'One size fits all, some better than others.' For something like this, I think the only way to know is to order them and try them out for yourself.

Although I didn't like the product, I've got nothing but praise for their customer service. The return window is only 14 days, but you can return them even if they've been used. That's exactly what I did and I got my refund as soon as they received the package. Given that, I'd say that it's worth giving GymPaws a try. They didn't work for me, but they seem to work for a lot of people. Although I only had them a short time, they felt sturdy and well-made enough to last a while. But try them on every sort of gear you regularly use before the return window shuts, especially if you're transitioning from regular gloves.
text_fidelity_b: GymPaws Real Leather Hand Pad Workout Glove Alternative | Hygienic n' Washable | Slightly Padded Palm w 4 Finger Loop SweatProof Back | Mens | Womens

Base+ Standing Desk Balance Board Aluminum Bamboo Wobble Board Ergonomic Office Standing Desk Accessories Wooden Balancing Platform footrest Easy Gentle 360 Motion Silver I've had this board a few weeks now, and I really enjoy it. I use my standing desk so much more now because the motion this board allows is actually fun. The board is very sturdy and mostly stays in place pretty well.

I have two complaints:

1. The surface is hard, so my feet get sore after standing on it for more than 30-45 minutes. I just ordered a small anti-fatigue standing mat that I'll have to cut to fit this board - maybe that will help. But I wish this board came with the option of a correctly-sized cushioned mat. If my feet weren't in pain, I'd probably stand on this more than half time, if not full time.

2. The description says "Stand Still | gently rock, tip, twist | aggressively balance, move & surf". I bought this model specifically because it said "twist". But it doesn't twist. The bottom of the ball is grippy rubber with knobs that make it even grippier, especially on the thin commercial carpet typically found in offices. The grippy rubber knobs are good for keeping it in place, but they completely prevent the board from twisting. You can force it to twist a little bit if you need to move it 1/2" forward or back, but you can not absent-mindedly twist while you're working. Also, while technically you can tip / rock forward and back, really the only motion that's at all natural is rocking side to side. It's really good for rocking side to side. Any other motion requires enough effort to make it a distraction from working.

I'll keep this, because I really do enjoy the motion, and this is a very high quality board for this price point. But I'll probably also order a Fluidstance board because I really want the twisting motion, and I need a higher weight limit, so I'll end up ordering their top-of-the-line, which is ~4.5 times the price of this board. Alas. If only this board actually twisted....
text_fidelity_b: Base+ Standing Desk Balance Board Aluminum Bamboo Wobble Board Ergonomic Office Standing Desk Accessories Wooden Balancing Platform footrest Easy Gentle 360 Motion Silver

text_fidelity_a:
Saver Pad Set I had an accident on my skateboard yesterday, hit my elbow pretty hard and quit for the day. I was going to wait for this protective gear before I started practicing Ollies or doing anything else risky, but my sore elbow was a good reminder to wait for the proper equipment to use before something like that (or worse) happened again.
This set of knee, elbow and wrist protectors is fairly well-made although light. The only thing I really don't like is the logo. After years in graphic-arts I have decided that I truly dislike high-visibility logos so I remove them by sanding or cutting them off. In the case of this "Triple-eight" with a horrible intersection of 3 eights the best method was flat black enamel paint that seems to have obliterated everything except the raised portions of the embroidery. Otherwise it's all black and low key. (This was my intent when I bought this kit and it worked well. Yay!)
The fit is fairly good for a mass-produced set of items, the big factor and the determination for S-M-L being the hand and wrist-guard, which I ordered Large. It's a little loose, but I have all sorts of foam sheets and leather pieces to custom-fit these important pieces, even to reinforcing the external portions as required. The knee and elbow pads are sort of a one-size-fits-all, but the same rules for modification apply.
Essentially, a very good buy for protection that is far better to have and not need than to really need and not have!
This is important stuff to wear, because a skateboard can become very dangerous suddenly without any warning. This kit, in conjunction with a decent helmet and good shoes (skate shoes) can make the difference in protecting those parts of your body that won't function very well unless they move freely without pain. Try being an artist or musician with a broken wrist. Try driving you car or riding your bike with a bad elbow or knee. It's in your best interest to protect yourself, because nobody else will, and if you still haven't figured it out getting hurt costs $$$!
text_fidelity_b: Saver Pad Set

text_fidelity_a:
United Cutlery Bushmaster Survival Knife I went through and read the good and the bad reviews. Taking all that into account and knowing what I know about knives, which as a retired chef is quite a bit, I decided to take a chance on this one.

First, even after reading the numerous reviews and manufacturer's info, I was astounded by the length of this knife. It is LONG. Not only is this knife long, it's heavy.

Second, as many noted, the knife blade wasn't all that sharp when received. Again, noting my background as a retired chef, taking care of knives and bringing them from the land of the dead to an item with a wonderfully usuable blade isn't all that difficult providing you've the equipment to do so.

I honed the knife using the medium grit on my tri-stone about 10 minutes then moved to the fine grit stone. That put a good edge on it. While watching Firefly (http://www.amazon.com/Firefly-Complete-Blu-ray-Nathan-Fillion/dp/B001EN71CW/ref=sr_1_3?s=movies-tv&ie=UTF8&qid=1363822981&sr=1-3&keywords=firefly), I pulled out the tri-stone again and continued with the medium to fine grit honing getting an even better blade on it.

The scabbard is appropriate for the knife. That, to me, says a lot. There's a lot of knife, there's a lot of scabbard. One other reviewer succinctly defined the contents of the pockets on the scabbard. I needn't do the same. Nor shall I wax about which pieces are good and which aren't. Everybody's entitled to their own opinions about that. That said, I'm keeping "most" of the prepackaged stuff there. I'm sure over the course of a few trips I'll update, tweak and tune what I want, but for the time being, it all stays.

I'm very satisifed with this knife. I know while I'm backpacking, hiking or camping I'll keep it close at hand. My son's got HIS knife, Whetstone Usa Full Tang Stainless Steel Jungle Survival Knife, (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B003U7SC6O/ref=oh_details_o06_s00_i01?ie=UTF8&psc=1), I've got mine.

Happy honing.
text_fidelity_b: United Cutlery Bushmaster Survival Knife

text_fidelity_a: ESEE Authentic Model 4HM Fixed Blade Knife, Black Powder Blade, Micarta Handle, Leather Sheath I have experience with 4X ESEE knives, and there is a tool for every job - I love them all.  I bought this one to "downsize" from the ESEE Laser Strike which I found to be way too heavy to carry all day, and while a phenomenal knife, was not as well suited for smaller tasks.  This one I found to be the perfect size for just about everything you do in the outdoors.  Also, for folks with smaller hands, or a desire to work the blade more deftly, the smaller handle drops weight and is more easy to manipulate vs. it's larger cousins. After much experimentation, I've settled on carrying this knife as well as the tiny fisherman version which has a very small blade (2.5 inch) and is perfect for squirrel and fish work.  The two together cover most tasks well.  I also purchased an aftermarket fire steel with a kydex sheath which I added later. I then had to MOD the blade by ever-so-gently using an electric wire brush to remove just about an inch of the blade coating on the spine of the blade right near the handle so you can effectively spark the fire steel.  Now, that will require extra oil maintenance to prevent rust, but if you take care of your tools, they will take care of you.  I would love to see ESEE create a sheath which could house all three items (anybody listening?).  Now if you are bushcrafting, remember to always carry a folding saw (safer) or a small axe.  With those four tools, and a sharpening stone, you can rebuild civilization!  If you have never had an ESEE knife, you will love this, so don't hesitate as it is bomb proof and will last you forever.  If you could only have one blade and your life depended on it, this is the one.  I may make some videos on this knife and when I do, you can find them at "Thecameracommando" on youtube.  Cheers and happy camping!
text_fidelity_b: ESEE Authentic Model 4HM Fixed Blade Knife, Black Powder Blade, Micarta Handle, Leather Sheath

text_fidelity_a:
ALPS Mountaineering Meramac 4-Person Tent, Sage/Rust Having had, and liking, several ALPS Mountaineering products ([[ASIN:B004R7L7YU ALPS OutdoorZ Commander Backpack, 5250 Cubic Inches]] and [[ASIN:B006H1YL1U ALPS Mountaineering Stuff Sack]]), and being in the market for another tent, I chose the 4 Person tent knowing that (1) I'll never really need it to hold four people and (2), I will not be carrying this in my backpack. This tent was specifically bought for car camping.

I like that it has a carry case instead of stuff sack. I'm not quite certain why, but this just seems to make more sense to me. I'm probably less likely to forget the case. I'm also happy with the set up. Instead of sliding poles through a sleeve as several of my other tents do, this is simply a connect the poles, lay them out, put the ends into the stoppers and clip the tent to the poles. It's much easier going up and, if you were in a good location, you really wouldn't need to put in pegs and could freestand.

The one thing about this tent that I didn't like or understand is why they were put a pole under the fly and have you pull the fly up and over the erected tent like that. Honestly, I looked and looked at the instructions and did not see a single thing about that. YouTube came to the rescue in the form of "Mr. Tent".

Since I've not had the opportunity to actually test it out of yet - sure I could put it up in the livingroom and have "Camp InHouse", and I may yet do that, I'm going to leave this review as is and modify it in the future should the need arise. I do not anticipate any problems because I am familiar with the brand, style of tent and my expected usage.
text_fidelity_b: ALPS Mountaineering Meramac 4-Person Tent, Sage/Rust

text_fidelity_a: FlipKlip Treadmill Book Holder 1-Pak This is a product that I want to love, and wants to be useful...and comes very close- but just misses the mark.  I use it for holding open those sheet music books that a certain music book publisher (I won't name names but it kinda rhymes with Cal Centered)seems to refuse to put in spiral bound form... ARRRGH nothing worse than trying to play a guitar when the book keeps closing on you.  I've tried everything I can think of to keep the pages open.  Closepins, those metal music stand arms, metal 3 pronged page clips, paperclips, spring clips.... heck even rubberbands.  This little gadget is probably the best solution so far (but not perfect). It will hold the book open (yea) but often times with sheet music you gotta flip back and forth between pages- this is difficult (not impossible, but does mess up the flow of the music).  The pins do hold well and have not ripped any pages so far- but they are a bit long and always seem to fall on the one note that I'm unsure of.  I kinda modified the way I use this by only clamping down on side of the book, leaving the other side loose so I can fip pages easier.  It works, but not perfectly.  If I were using this for straight up reading, it would be a 5 star no brainer, but for music....well it earned 4 stars (I'm feeling generous as this is the best solution I have found so far)

text_fidelity_a:
Trangia Fuel Bottle Headline pretty well sums it up. This bottle and pour spout is much easier to use than the soda bottle or HEET bottle I was using before. Pouring fuel into the Trangia burner is far easier, it won't come open when inside or strapped to the outside of my pack. This bottle is STURDY, I don't worry about puncturing it like I did with the soda bottles. The seals are meant for alcohol use, so no concerns about a seal on a soda bottle going wonky and spilling fuel(aka my coffee and non-crunchy pasta) when miles from civilization either.

Possible downside is weight. I'm not lugging the kitchen sink into the back country, but I also don't do long hikes and I'm not cutting the handle off my toothbrush to save 0.3 grams. If that's you, the soda bottle is probably a better bet.

These bottles will also work with gasoline and kerosene. US law changed and so this kind of bottle can't be advertised for gasoline use anymore, but it's exactly the same bottle from before the law change, and is still used with kero and gasoline in the rest of the world. YMMV, this is not medical or legal advice, insert standard disclaimer here, etc etc.

One last thought, the .3l bottle has been great for single day or overnight hikes and is of course the lightest. Longer than that and I'd want a bigger fuel bottle. We like our coffee and tea and boil a lot of water. If you're just heating up coffee water or something on a day hike, then as long as the O-ring seal in your burner cap is good you probably don't need to carry any extra fuel at all.

Five stars, wish I had bought it sooner.

Edit: Just bought the 1L version. Should have bought it when I bought the 0.3l version!
text_fidelity_b: Trangia Fuel Bottle

text_fidelity_a:
A SLICE RED Packable Backpack Small Waterproof Travel Hiking Daypack I gave the A SLICE RED Ultra Lightweight Packable Backpack (In black) 5 stars as you can see.

Here is my situation. I hunt. Don't find much but I hunt a lot and I have this big professional camo honkering GREAT backpack. I could survive everything but a nuclear war with only that thing. And that's a good thing...but...

I also often hunt out of a portable tree stand and that big old pro back unit is just a mess in that situation. Clunky, And it's heavy! So I was really looking forward to my new backpack for the purpose. I moved the essentials from my pro pack to the new one and it's exactly what I was looking for.

The A SLICE RED Ultra Lightweight Packable Backpack is a baby backpack for sure. It's a dufflebag put together in the shape of a backpack actually. When you get it stuffed it becomes the backpack. It has a front pocket. A mesh side pocket, good for a bottle of water or necessary paper..whatever you like. And the interior, at least for my purposes is plenty roomy. I have room to spare. That surprised me. Unlike the big boys this little pack adds zero weight to whatever you put in there. That's a bonus. The zippers worked fine, btw. Backstraps are adjustable. A little flimsy compared to high dollar, but they don't slip

Is it rough and tumble? Probably not. I wouldn't trust it in rough country with briars and such...but for normal use, it's fine. It is a day hiker or a day hunter. From the cost point and utility it's a fine choice for normal wear. I'm very pleased.
text_fidelity_b: A SLICE RED Packable Backpack Small Waterproof Travel Hiking Daypack

text_fidelity_a: VX-Power Seated Elliptical Bike - Electric Under Desk Mini Elliptical Machine, Feet Massager, Compact Pedal Exerciser for Seniors, Home Office Leg Workout Exercise Equipment w/Remote & LCD Display Okay, I think this elliptical is a decent, portable version, especially for those without room for a full size machine (would love one, but really could not fit one in my house!).  The problem I have had with it is the roller massagers.  Don't get me wrong, I love a good foot massage...but rollers don't work for me and my sensitive soles.  If they were tiny, like no larger than a BB pellet, that might work, but these feel honkin' BIG against the soles of my feet and they HURT.  Plus, they are still right there in the pedal even when you aren't getting a message.  I have dry eye syndrome and have a kind of space age-looking eye cover that has similar massager balls that goes around and "squeeze" my eyeballs and these don't bother me.  I just can't handle a lot of things against the soles of my feet - rocks felt through my shoes nearly bring me to tears, that's how bad it is with my feet.  So...I did my best to work around the issue with thickly padded pieces that fit over the pedal area to nullify the feeling of the massage balls against my skin and that's working, but I shouldn't have to do that.  I do enjoy using the machine - I am older and need the exercise and this is good for getting in steps even when the weather is bad and I can't just walk in pouring rain, 60 MPH winds or really cold weather.  Just wish the massager part was made differently.  Heck, I have a "foot massager" that is like a giant Tens unit pad that transmits a small shock of electricity to the skin and deeper, to the muscle tissue.  That actually gives me a really decent "massage" that soothes and calms my aching feet if I've been walking/standing too long.  I mention this as a possible suggestion for a different type of massage that won't require large rollers!  Maybe if you don't suffer from sensitive feet this machine will work great for you just as it is.

GERBER Folding Spade w/Sheath - Model 5940 The Gerber folding shovel is really top notch. Its quality construction is much like any other Gerber/Fiskars equipment I've owned - it doesn't disappoint.

The shovel I have is actually a little more agressively pointed than in the pictures, so I'm not sure if Gerber has addressed this as an issue or if the pictures were off.

The top of the handle is high density polycarbonate plastic and has a horizontal design like a spade should have. You can still use the verticle part of the steel handle if you wish, but there isn't much of it. The plastic will absorb some shock compared to steel-only, and it won't freeze to your hands, etc. The polycarb handle folds down on itself, so that it actually has 3 segments (instead of several designs which have 2 segments). This means you can stow the shovel in the included cordura nylon belt pouch which is no bigger than the shovel head itself. The handle pivot point locks and since it's square, doesn't rotate or twist easily. The steel which connects the blade to the handle fits nicely inside the A angle cutout of the handle, so when collapsed it is really thin.

The blade is high quality steel with the hinged handle connected at the top. This does limit the depth of the shovel a little, but I don't believe it's much of a factor, except maybe in really solid soil where you lose a little verticle travel when the ground butts up against the hinge.

It's very compact, light, comes with a solid belt sheath (easily convertible to pack carry) and stows away easily since it's so thin. I can put it in the side pockets of my doors or in the very small space above my rear wheel well without any problems (Trailblazer 4x4).

I really can find no fault with this item, it delivers on all fronts: usability, quality, compact storage, and rugged design. I will almost certainly be keeping one in both cars and in my 72 Hour survival kit. They are even reasonably priced. 5 Stars.
text_fidelity_b: GERBER Folding Spade w/Sheath - Model 5940

text_fidelity_a:
Primus | OmniFuel Multi Fuel Backpacking Stove Kit | High-Heat Output Stove with Fuel Bottle & ErgoPump [[VIDEOID:3e35f8b3c9ff2db1bc3918716d231bf8]] I have owned three single-burner camp stoves.

My first stove was an MSR XGK, which was lightweight, but was NOISY (like a jet engine) and could be adjusted to either OFF or INCINERATE. As an earlier model XGK it shared the light weight of its successors, but was not compact or easily stowed because it had an unflexible fuel pipe instead of a fuel hose. Those factors eventually made me sell it.

My second stove was a Coleman Exponent Apex II camp stove. This stove is quiet, compact, pretty lightweight, and simmers. But it's been 10 years or so and it now needs some maintenance parts, but Coleman doesn't make or sell them anymore. (That, by the way, is a real pisser, because I am the descendant of several generations of outdoorspeople who expected to inherit a Coleman product, maintain and use it for 50 years, and pass it down to their children for infinity.)

These experiences influenced my choice of a new camp stove. Simmering may not be for the real rugged types, but I need more versatility than just boiling water to reconstitute freeze-dried meals. Noise is something I want to escape from when I am enjoying nature, and I'd like to expect (although I'm often disappointed) that my fellow campers do too. Fuel source is another consideration: I was thinking of an ultralight bottled gas (as in not liquid) fuel stove, but just don't like the idea of all of those disposable cans tossed in a landfill (they aren't recyclable in my area, and I think I've heard about far distant lands that are littered with the things). I have also read that bottled gas stoves don't perform in cold or at altitude (although K2 is not in my immediate plans).

Before getting the Primus OmniLite, I considered a new MSR XGK. [[ASIN:B00G3PALBY MSR XGK EX Multi-Fuel Stove]] Cascade Designs (maker of the MSR XGK EX) is based in the Pacific Northwest and the MSR XGK EX is __ Made In The USA __ a BIG PLUS for me. Unlike my old version, reviewers say that the EX can burn at a simmer. But, many reviewers are suspicious of the XGK's plastic pump, and they also comment on how noisy the XGK still is ("jet engine" remains the theme).

A word on noisy stoves: For those who share my ethos about noise pollution, there is a product called QuietStove[[ASIN:B008129SEI QUIETSTOVE® SILENT MUTER DAMPER CAP for PRIMUS OMNIFUEL BACKPACKING CAMPING STOVE]] that probably does help a lot.

So, I opted for the Primus OmniLite, and since I might as well go all-in, I got the Ti version. This stove is light, portable, multi-fuel capable, reasonably quiet, simmers, and has a metal (mostly) pump. I have not yet taken it on a trip, but will update this review when I do. I did get the QuietStove module, which I will demonstrate on a video.
text_fidelity_b: Primus | OmniFuel Multi Fuel Backpacking Stove Kit | High-Heat Output Stove with Fuel Bottle & ErgoPump
